1	# ADR-020: Declarative package convergence — a package replicates as (name, origin), and repository configuration follows the packages approved from it
2	
3	Status: Draft
4	
5	Date: 2026-07-23
6	
7	## TL;DR
8	
9	The source captures a manifest of package-related items; the target diffs its own state against it and converges using `apt`, `snap` and `flatpak` themselves — package databases are never rsynced. A package replicates as (name, origin), not name: the review decides packages and apt config, while repositories, their keys, pins, flatpak remotes and blocks — apt holds, snap refresh holds, flatpak masks — are all derived, replicated because the software they serve is and never reviewed at all. Four independent jobs (`apt_sync`, `snap_sync`, `flatpak_sync`, `manual_installs_sync`) each run plan then review then apply inside their own `execute()`, every change approved before it is made and the questions batched into one screen per manager per action where the logic permits.
10	
11	## Context
12	
13	Phase 2 must replicate presence, version and provenance of packages across apt, snap and flatpak, plus the repository/keyring/pin/remote configuration those installs depend on. Package data under `~/.var/app`, `~/snap/<app>/common` and dotfiles is Phase 1 `folder_sync` territory; this ADR concerns the packages and the configuration that governs where they come from.
14	
15	Provenance is the hard part, because a package name is offered by more than one vendor: `firefox` exists in Ubuntu's archive and in Mozilla's own repository, and `org.mozilla.firefox` on Flathub and Flathub-beta. Matching by name alone replicates the name and inverts the provenance, silently and at exit 0. Replication is therefore of (name, origin), and the configuration that makes an origin reachable is mechanism serving that guarantee rather than something the user is asked about — a repository ticked without its package does nothing, a package ticked without its repository cannot be installed, and the pairing was never expressible in a checkbox list.
16	
17	The review boundary is the manager: each package job captures its own diff and surfaces it for decision before it applies anything, and no review spans more than a single manager's items — which keeps four deliberately independent jobs independent rather than binding them to a shared review with a common ordering and failure surface. The normative obligations these decisions imply are stated as checkable articles in [package-sync-conformance-criteria.md](../planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md) (`PKG-FR-*`, `PKG-NG-*`); this ADR records the decisions, not a second rule set.
18	
19	## Decision
20	
21	### Convergence model (D-01)
22	
23	The source captures a manifest; the target diffs its own state against it and converges using `apt`, `snap` and `flatpak` themselves. `/var/lib/dpkg`, `/var/lib/snapd` and the flatpak OSTree store are never rsynced — the package managers stay authoritative for their own state.
24	
25	### Item model (D-02)
26	
27	An item is something the user can meaningfully decide about, carrying a stable identity through one diff → decide → apply pipeline. The item classes are the apt package, the apt config file, the snap, the snap channel, the flatpak ref, the unreproducible/manual install, and — for removal only — the apt source file and the apt pin file. A flatpak remote is not an item (D-41), and neither is a block — an apt hold, a snap refresh hold or a flatpak mask.
28	
29	A block keeps an identity of its own so the converge order (install before hold, masks after refs) and failure reporting can name it, but it is **derived**, not decided: it replicates because the software it applies to does, exactly as a pin does. Replicating every one costs nothing and cannot get a per-item derivation wrong, while asking about one separately let the user contradict the answer they gave about the software itself. A block that freezes an installed copy — an apt hold, a snap refresh hold — is not registered for software the target does not end the run with; a flatpak mask is a rule about what may be installed and still lands. An apt hold naming a package its own machine does not have freezes nothing while refusing every later install of that name: the run ends, naming the package and the machine. Mechanism the user has no basis to judge — repository files, signing keys, pins, flatpak remotes, and a transient guard a run sets and clears — is not an item and is the job's own business to keep correct (D-34, D-36, D-37, D-41).
30	
31	### Manifest content for apt (D-03)
32	
33	The manifest carries the manually-installed set from `apt-mark showmanual`, not the full dpkg selection set; apt resolves dependencies on the target.
34	
35	### Version policy (D-04, D-05)
36	
37	Versions float to whatever the target's repos currently offer, and a version mismatch is a reported diff class rather than a forced change — which is why there is no version-pinning machinery. The one exception inside apt is a held package, which takes the source's exact version, because an apt hold blocks install, upgrade and removal alike and so carries "do not move this off the version that works". This is a product rule; its intent is owned by [package-sync-user-requirements.md](../planning/package-sync-user-requirements.md#the-model). Deliberate `preferences.d` pins still travel (D-36) even though versions float.
38	
39	### Revision/scope convergence (D-06)
40	
41	The snap manifest carries name + channel + revision; the flatpak manifest carries ref + origin + user/system scope. Snap converges revision and channel, because snap is the only ecosystem that embeds the version in its per-user data path (`~/snap/<app>/<rev>`), so both machines on the same revision is what lets `folder_sync` mirror that data cleanly. snapd auto-refreshes in the background and could move a snap off the converged revision mid-run, so the orchestrator pauses snapd's automatic refresh across the sync window on both hosts, restoring each host's prior setting on cleanup and relying on a timeout so a crashed run leaves no pause behind. This gates only auto-refresh, not the explicit convergence, and never leaves a standing block on any manager's auto-update once a run ends.
42	
43	### Decision shape and direction (D-07)
44	
45	The default is a three-way decision: apply / skip once / skip always. A `REPORT_ONLY` item takes NO answer at all — it converges in neither direction and records nothing, so both answers would leave both machines identical; such items are printed, grouped by the `DiffClass` that caused them, each group carrying the remedy where there is one. "Apply" is direction-dependent: missing on target means install/add/enable, extra means remove/delete/disable, different on both means change the target to match the source. Two cases take **two** answers — act, or skip once — and record nothing: an apt source or pin removal (D-37), and the repository/remote-conflict overwrite prompts (D-37, D-41); a flatpak remote is never asked about (D-41). The grammar these screens and answers follow — hostnames not source/target, one answer per key, the answers read as a set — is specified in [package-sync.md](../system/package-sync.md) and its articles.
46	
47	### Machine-local decision file (D-08, D-08a, D-09, D-10, D-43)
48	
49	One file per manager lives at `~/.config/pc-switcher/<manager>.decisions.yaml`, never synced, excluded from `folder_sync` non-overridably and outside `config_sync`. An entry on machine M makes the item inert on M in both roles — not pushed when M is the source, not installed or removed when M is the target. It is written on the machine whose copy the answer keeps: an install declined for good on the source, a declined removal or overwrite on the target. An overwrite is the one direction whose holder the run's own direction cannot name — both machines have the item and the recorder takes the other role next sync — so an item both machines have is read back from both files and filtered out of both inventories (D-08a). An entry lasts as long as its item is on the machine holding it, and is dropped once that machine no longer has it (D-43), including when this run's own approved work took it (the collateral case D-30 allows). A dead entry is not the cautious option: it acts in both roles, so one naming absent software goes on refusing to install it there for good. The check is a positive statement that the machine lacks the item, never absence from the narrower inventory the diff was built from; a check that cannot answer drops nothing. Software that returns is a new item, reviewed again.
50	
51	### Repository configuration is derived mechanism (D-11, D-12, D-13, D-14)
52	
53	`/etc/apt` is not file-mirrored: a `--delete` mirror would wipe the target's own machine-specific sources, and it is not an inventory of reviewed items. Four buckets cover every file: derived from approved packages (repository files, their keyrings, conflict-free overwrites of a repository on both machines — D-34, D-37); always synced (every `preferences.d` pin — D-36 — and the distribution's own source files — D-38); reviewed with two answers (repository and pin removals, the repository-conflict overwrite — D-07, D-37); and reviewed with the full three-way decision (`apt.conf.d` — D-37). Only files apt itself reads are captured, compared or written, by each fragment directory's own extension and filename rule (D-13; the `.save`, `.distUpgrade`, `.dpkg-dist` and editor backups those directories collect are left alone, since treating one as configuration would propose a change apt would never act on — [measurements](considerations/adr-020-apt-esm-and-snap-measurements.md)). A repository's signing key travels with it byte-for-byte from the source, never re-fetched from a vendor (a fresh fetch would silently substitute whatever the vendor serves today); the same governs a flatpak remote's ostree keyring (D-41). A repository whose key cannot be made to work is reported, not written. Every repository, key, pin and remote an approved item needs is provisioned before the install that needs it (D-14): for apt the `/etc/apt` group converges ahead of the first `apt-get install`, for flatpak the derived remote writes run ahead of the first `flatpak install`.
54	
55	### Job split into four jobs (D-15, D-16, D-17, D-18)
56	
57	Four jobs — `apt_sync`, `snap_sync`, `flatpak_sync`, `manual_installs_sync` — are four separate `SyncJob`s, never merged into one `package_sync`, over one shared core extracted while building. The core holds what all four use: the item taxonomy, the plan/review/apply order, the decision flow, the batched TUI review, the machine-local file I/O and the read-failure guard (ADR-022). Each manager's own item shapes and diff stay in that manager's module — one manager's diff on the shared base would make the other three inherit inputs they never supply. All four run before `folder_sync` so software is provisioned before its data lands (decisive for flatpak, where `~/.local/share/flatpak` must exist before `~/.var/app` arrives); a snippet-installed program writes its own stock defaults as a package does. `manual_installs_sync` owns everything no package manager can reproduce and carries its own enable flag.
58	
59	### Batched review inside each job (D-24)
60	
61	Each package job runs plan then review then apply inside its own `execute()` and converges only what the review approved. Batching — one screen per manager per action — is a strong preference, applied where the logic permits and abandoned where it does not: a job never turns a batch into a question per item, and never complicates or omits its logic to avoid another round. A job may ask again, including after it has begun writing, when the answer it needs rests on facts this run's own changes invalidated or that no read could establish before the first write; correctness outranks batching, always. `apt_sync` asks in rounds, and only `apt_sync`. Three of its questions are scoped to the work this run APPROVES rather than proposes — a repository not raised for deletion while an approved-surviving package still uses it, a repository conflict raised only for a file an approved package makes travel, and a package marked as the target's own — none decidable while the plan is built and all decidable once the first round's answers exist: a second round, same sitting, nothing written yet. The one thing unknowable before writing is the collateral of an install whose repository this run itself writes (D-40): a third round, asked once, before the first of those installs. The other three jobs have one round. No review spans two managers (D-15), so there is no shared review phase and no coordinator.
62	
63	### Diff taxonomy (D-25)
64	
65	Conflicts, mismatches and unavailability are diff classes inside the job's own review: missing-on-target, extra-on-target, version-mismatch (both versions shown), origin-mismatch, origin-unavailable, unreproducible. `ORIGIN_MISMATCH` covers a package or ref installed on both machines from different vendors. `REPO_UNAVAILABLE` means the source's origin cannot be provided on the target — a statement about provenance, not about whether apt printed a candidate. There is no per-package echo of a pin or a hold: D-35 checks a pin against the target's real state, and echoing it onto every package it names would make a pinned target-only package impossible to remove.
66	
67	### Transactional repository convergence (D-27 boundary)
68	
69	The `/etc/apt` group is the one place D-27's continue-and-report model does not apply: it is transactional, and a group whose metadata refresh fails leaves `/etc/apt` as it found it. Continuing past a bad write would leave the target's package manager unusable, and automatic snapshot rollback does not arrive until Phase 7.
